entity.name: Carl Linnaeus
entity.description: The man who named every living thing on Earth. A Swedish pastor's son who gave a flower whenever he cried as a child, Linnaeus invented binomial nomenclature — the two-word naming system (Homo sapiens, Canis lupus) still used for every species. He even designated himself as the type specimen for the human race.

story.name: Carl Linnaeus
story.description: A child calmed by flowers nearly becomes a cobbler's apprentice, treks 2,000 km through Lapland cataloguing 100 new plants, publishes the system that names every species on Earth, and designates himself as humanity's type specimen.

moments.name: Carl Linnaeus Is Born to a Flower-Obsessed Pastor in Rural Sweden
moments.subtitle: A child who could only be calmed by holding a flower would grow up to name every plant on Earth
moments.description: On 23 May 1707, Carl Linnaeus was born in the village of Rashult in Smaland, southern Sweden. His father Nils was a Lutheran curate and amateur botanist who gave young Carl his own garden plot and calmed the crying infant by handing him flowers. The family name itself was invented: Nils adopted the Latinate "Linnaeus" after a giant lime tree on the family homestead when he enrolled at Lund University. At school, Carl's teachers told his father the boy would never become a scholar. One teacher disagreed, recognizing the boy's botanical obsession — and redirected him from the priesthood toward medicine and science.

moments.name: A Second-Year Student Begins Lecturing to 300 People at Uppsala University
moments.subtitle: The professor's 24 children needed a tutor, and Linnaeus needed a stage
moments.description: In May 1730, Professor Olof Rudbeck the Younger selected Carl Linnaeus — still only a second-year student — to deliver official botany lectures at Uppsala University. Linnaeus's thesis on plant sexual reproduction had caught Rudbeck's attention, and the young man soon drew audiences of 300. Linnaeus moved into Rudbeck's household as tutor to three of his 24 children. That winter, dissatisfied with existing plant classification, Linnaeus began designing his own system based on counting stamens and pistils — the kernel of what would become the most widely used classification system in the history of biology.

moments.name: Linnaeus Treks 2,000 Kilometers Through Lapland and Discovers 100 New Plants
moments.subtitle: A 25-year-old walks to the Arctic and back with pressed flowers and a horse jawbone revelation
moments.description: On 12 May 1732, Carl Linnaeus departed Uppsala on foot and horseback for a six-month, 2,000-kilometer expedition through Lapland. Funded by a grant from the Royal Society of Sciences, the 25-year-old catalogued about 100 previously unidentified plant species, studied the customs of the Sami people, and collected specimens of mosses, lichens, birds, and rocks. Near Gavle, he found the twinflower (Linnaea borealis) that would become his favorite plant. A horse jawbone on the roadside sparked his insight into classifying mammals by teeth and teats. The expedition produced Flora Lapponica, considered the first proto-modern Flora.

moments.name: Linnaeus Publishes Systema Naturae and Invents Modern Taxonomy
moments.subtitle: An 11-page pamphlet in the Netherlands launches a system that will name every species on Earth
moments.description: In 1735, Carl Linnaeus published the first edition of Systema Naturae in the Netherlands — an 11-page pamphlet that classified the natural world into kingdoms, classes, orders, genera, and species. Over subsequent editions (the final 12th edition ran to 2,400 pages), Linnaeus formalized binomial nomenclature: the two-word Latin naming system (genus + species) still used for every organism on Earth. Linnaeus classified roughly 7,700 plant species and 4,400 animal species, including Homo sapiens — a name he coined. He even designated himself as the type specimen for the human species, a designation that technically still stands.

moments.name: Carl Linnaeus Dies as Europe's Most Celebrated Scientist
moments.subtitle: The man who named all life left behind 40,000 specimens and a system that outlived every rival
moments.description: On 10 January 1778, Carl Linnaeus died in Uppsala, Sweden, at the age of 70. He had suffered a series of strokes beginning in 1774 that gradually robbed him of his faculties. By the time of his death, Linnaeus was one of the most acclaimed scientists in Europe, having been ennobled as Carl von Linne in 1761. His personal collections — over 40,000 plant, animal, and mineral specimens — were purchased by an English naturalist and became the foundation of the Linnean Society of London. Today, every species described in biology still carries a Linnaean binomial name, making his system arguably the most enduring intellectual framework in science.
